passage: Note by Amandeep, career counsellor. Parul brought two offer letters on Thursday and asked me to check her thinking, not to choose for her. On a sheet she listed learning, pay, stability, commute and team, then said aloud, "What do I care about most? Learning, then team. Pay matters, but I can live on either." She gave learning a weight of 5, team 4, pay 3, stability 3, commute 2, scored each offer out of 5, and multiplied. The large firm came to 61, the smaller one to 67. "Huh," she said. "I expected the big name to win." She spent ten minutes re-testing her weights and kept them. I asked nothing more. She will phone the smaller firm's manager tomorrow with two questions.

qa.q: What were the two totals on Parul's sheet?
qa.a: The large firm came to 61 and the smaller one to 67.

qa.q: What is Parul feeling when the smaller firm comes out ahead?
qa.a: Surprised and a little unsettled: she says 'Huh', admits she expected the big name to win, and re-tests her weights.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Parul use alongside the matrix, and why?
qa.a: She could talk to current employees at both firms, because the scores rest on her own guesses while employees can share facts the letters leave out.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Parul's method?
qa.a: Amandeep watches a graduate who tests her own weights instead of asking to be told, which is why Amandeep asks nothing more.

grounding: Shows a weighted decision matrix: two offers scored on several criteria with personal weights, leaving the smaller company slightly ahead.

passage: Call me Suraj the list-maker, Afreen. You asked how I decided, so here is the honest version. I took a page and drew a line down the middle for each offer. Pune: better projects, a team lead who writes papers, a higher package. My home city: I can stay with my parents, a friendly manager, a little less money. Twelve lines in all. And funny thing, the moment I finished I saw the list only said what I already felt: I wanted Pune. But one line surprised me. Under Pune's drawbacks I had written "deposit, first month's rent, furniture". I had not counted the cost of moving at all. It did not change my mind, but it made me ask the company what help they give with joining. That one line was worth the page.

qa.q: What did Suraj write under Pune's drawbacks?
qa.a: Suraj wrote 'deposit, first month's rent, furniture'.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when the list matched what was already felt?
qa.a: Suraj felt a quiet recognition, almost amused and reassured, because the list only said what Suraj already felt: wanting Pune.

qa.q: What alternative approach could test the wish for Pune, and why?
qa.a: Ask which choice would be regretted in two years, because a list counts items while a regret test checks the feeling behind them.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Suraj's story?
qa.a: Afreen asked how Suraj decided and gets an honest answer, so Afreen learns that the list mostly confirmed a feeling and only added one new fact.

grounding: Shows a pros-and-cons list that mainly confirmed an existing preference but revealed a forgotten cost of relocating.

passage: Paulo spread two offer letters on a café table in Porto, next to his sister Dalia's laptop. He tried to stop staring at the salary lines. "Forget the numbers for a minute," he said quietly. "Where do I want to be in three years?" He answered himself: someone who can design systems, not only close tickets. Company A paid more, but its team was young and rushed, with nobody to look over his work. Company B paid less, yet it had Ines, a senior engineer who reviewed code line by line and taught juniors. "Who will teach me?" he said. "That matters more than the first year's package." Dalia refilled his coffee and said nothing. That evening he emailed Company B to accept.

qa.q: Who is the senior engineer at Company B?
qa.a: Ines is the senior engineer who reviewed code line by line.

qa.q: What is Paulo feeling as he tries to look past the salary lines?
qa.a: Paulo is torn but growing sure: he wants to become someone who can design systems, and that wish pulls him toward mentoring.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Paulo use to double-check his choice, and why?
qa.a: He could ask a current junior at Company B about the mentoring, because his values point to Ines but a junior can confirm whether teaching really happens.

qa.q: How does Dalia see Paulo's decision?
qa.a: Dalia sits beside him, refills his coffee and says nothing, which suggests she wants Paulo to reach the answer in his own words.

grounding: Shows values-first planning: asking what matters over three years and preferring the team with mentoring over a bigger starting package.

subtype: Approach: talking to current employees at both firms [Action]
passage: Note by Jagdish, mentor. On Monday Rashmi showed me two messages she had sent through a professional network, one to an engineer at each firm that had offered her a job. Each asked the same three things: how heavy the workload gets, how much people learn, and how appraisals work. By Wednesday both had replied. One wrote that sprints end late on Thursdays, learning is mostly on your own, and appraisal comes once a year. The other described weekly code reviews, a small course budget, and appraisal every six months. Rashmi copied both answers into a table. "None of this was in the offer letters," she said. I suggested nothing. She will ask each HR team about appraisal timing before Friday.

qa.q: Which three things did Rashmi ask each employee?
qa.a: She asked how heavy the workload gets, how much people learn, and how appraisals work.

qa.q: What is Rashmi feeling as she copies the replies into a table?
qa.a: She seems relieved and curious: she says none of this was in the offer letters, and she is glad to have real details.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rashmi try to check what she heard, and why?
qa.a: She could ask each HR team the same questions in writing, because two individual views may be a little biased and an official reply is easier to compare.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see Rashmi's approach?
qa.a: Jagdish watches a graduate collecting facts before choosing, and holds back suggestions so that the decision stays with Rashmi.

grounding: Shows a graduate contacting current employees at two firms and learning details about work, learning and appraisal that the offer letters omit.

subtype: Approach: choosing by brand name alone [Pitfall]
passage: Thursday night. Eight months into the famous company, and I finally wrote it down. When the offer came, Nirmala Aunty from next door brought sweets and my cousins told everyone the name. I never asked what my role was. Today I closed forty-one tickets by pasting the same replies. The team is called support. My manager says the developer track has no openings this year. I have not written a single line of real code since August, and my old college projects are already going stale. Everyone still says "You're so lucky." I nod. I feel stuck between a name people admire and a job that teaches me nothing. — Lokesh

qa.q: What did Lokesh do with tickets today?
qa.a: Lokesh closed forty-one tickets by pasting the same replies.

qa.q: What is Lokesh feeling at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Lokesh feels stuck and quietly disappointed, caught between a name people admire and work that teaches nothing.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Lokesh have used when the offer came, and why?
qa.a: Lokesh could have asked what the role involved and how people grew in it, because the name told nothing about the daily work.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Aunty see Lokesh's job?
qa.a: Nirmala Aunty sees the famous name that earned sweets, not the tickets, so that pride may make it harder for Lokesh to say how things really are.

grounding: Shows choosing an offer for the company's fame without checking the role, followed by finding the work repetitive with little growth.

subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis with too many criteria [Pitfall]
passage: Dilnaz's spreadsheet had thirteen criteria on Monday night. On Tuesday she added the fourteenth, "quality of office chairs", and reweighted everything. On Wednesday she changed learning from 20 percent to 18 and pay from 12 to 14. Her flatmate Darshan looked over her shoulder at midnight. "The deadline is Friday at five." "I know, I know, one more pass." On Thursday she dropped chairs and added "friendly seniors". On Friday afternoon she was still deciding which weighting felt fair. At five past five, an email arrived: the offer she had leaned toward had lapsed, since no reply was received. She stared at the sheet, its cells all neatly coloured, and then at the one offer left.

qa.q: Which criterion did Dilnaz add as the fourteenth?
qa.a: She added 'quality of office chairs' as the fourteenth.

qa.q: What is Dilnaz feeling as she stares at the sheet after the email?
qa.a: She is stunned and regretful: the offer she had leaned toward has lapsed while she kept tinkering.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Dilnaz have used, and why?
qa.a: She could have fixed five criteria and a decision time in advance, because a limit on the process keeps the deadline from disappearing.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Dilnaz's nightly reweighting?
qa.a: Darshan sees the deadline approaching while she keeps adjusting, and reminds her at midnight that it is Friday at five, though she asks for one more pass.

grounding: Shows analysis paralysis: extra criteria and nightly reweighting until the acceptance deadline passes and one offer is lost.

subtype: Approach: inversion asking which choice would be regretted [Thinking]
passage: On the evening train out of Leipzig, Felix stared at the dark window and put a different question to himself. Not "which job is better?" but "which choice would I regret more in two years?" He pictured himself then, still in the tidy old role, doing the same reports, watching his friend Abebe's photos from the start-up's messy first office. That picture made his chest tighten. Then he pictured the start-up folding and himself job-hunting again. That one hurt too, but it felt like something he could recover from. He typed a note to Abebe: "Staying still is the bigger regret. I'm taking the risk." Abebe replied in seconds with a thumbs-up and "Bring snacks to the office."

qa.q: Which question did Felix ask himself on the train?
qa.a: He asked which choice he would regret more in two years.

qa.q: What is Felix feeling when he pictures staying in the old role?
qa.a: Felix feels a tightening dread, since the picture of the same reports two years on makes his chest tighten.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Felix add before accepting, and why?
qa.a: He could imagine the start-up closing and check what he could do next, because that shows whether the risk is survivable.

qa.q: How might Abebe see Felix's decision?
qa.a: Abebe, whose photos show the start-up's messy first office, replies in seconds with a thumbs-up, so Abebe seems glad to see Felix join.

grounding: Shows inversion: asking which decision would feel worse in two years and seeing that staying stagnant would be the bigger regret.

subtype: Approach: negotiating with a deadline extension [Action]
passage:
Subject: Request for a short extension

Dear Baljeet,

Thank you again for the offer. I am very glad to have it and I want to answer properly. I have another decision still pending, and I expect to hear from them by Monday. Could I please have three more days, until Tuesday evening, to reply to you? In that time I plan to compare both offers on role, team and learning, and I will give you a clear yes or no by then. If the original date has to stand, I understand and will let you know.

Warm regards,
Yash

qa.q: How many extra days did Yash ask for?
qa.a: Yash asked for three more days.

qa.q: What is Yash feeling as the email is written?
qa.a: Yash feels grateful but a little nervous: the wording is warm and careful because Yash does not want to lose the offer by asking.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Yash use if the extension is refused, and why?
qa.a: Yash could do a quick pros-and-cons comparison at once, because a refusal shortens the time and a short structured list still allows an honest answer.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see this request?
qa.a: Baljeet reads a polite, honest message that names a reason and a plan, which makes it easier to say yes than a vague delay would.

grounding: Shows politely asking one company for a few more days, saying another decision is pending, and promising a clear answer without misleading anyone.

subtype: Approach: scenario planning for the worse case [Thinking]
passage: Nandini took a sheet of paper to the balcony of her Bengaluru flat and wrote at the top: "Start-up shuts down next March." Her flatmate Tanuja, home from her own shift, sat on the railing with a cup of tea. "Morbid," she said. "Just checking," said Nandini. She wrote three headings. Money: her rent and food for five months were already saved. Skills: the start-up would let her ship real features, which would look good on a résumé. People: two seniors from her internship had said to stay in touch. She counted, then wrote at the bottom: "I could find another job within a few months." The fear did not vanish, but it stopped feeling like a cliff. She went inside and signed the offer.

qa.q: What three headings did Nandini write?
qa.a: She wrote money, skills and people.

qa.q: What is Nandini feeling after she finishes the list?
qa.a: She feels calmer but not fearless: the fear did not vanish, but it stopped feeling like a cliff.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Nandini add, and why?
qa.a: She could ask the start-up how long its funding lasts, because imagining the worst case helps most when it is checked with real facts.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Nandini's exercise?
qa.a: Tanuja finds it morbid at first, calling it that aloud, but she sits with her tea and lets Nandini finish it.

grounding: Shows scenario planning for a worse case: imagining the start-up closing and checking savings, skills and contacts so that the risk seems manageable.

passage: Kashish, sit. You look worried about your offer, so let old Imran tell you mine. I was twenty-two. I accepted a job at a pump factory in Coimbatore, and a week later the letter arrived: joining location changed to Hosur. My first thought was to ignore it and hope. Then I thought, no. I wrote to the HR officer, Mrs Gill, and asked, "Please confirm in writing where I will work." Her reply took two days: the change was only for the training month, and the posting stayed Coimbatore. If it had said Hosur permanently, I had decided I would think again. It didn't. I joined, and the first thing I learned was to ask the question when the fact changes, not three months later.

qa.q: Where did the letter say the joining location had changed to?
qa.a: The letter said the joining location had changed to Hosur.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when the letter about the new location arrived?
qa.a: Imran felt uneasy and tempted to ignore it, hoping the problem would go away, before deciding to act.

qa.q: What choice did Imran make that worked, and why?
qa.a: Imran asked HR to confirm the location in writing rather than ignoring it, because a written answer gave a clear fact to base any further decision on.

qa.q: How might Mrs Gill have seen Imran's question?
qa.a: Mrs Gill received a calm, specific request and answered in two days, so she likely saw a new employee who wanted clarity rather than someone complaining.

grounding: Shows revising after new information: checking a changed joining location in writing and reconsidering only if the answer differed.
